\chapter{Easy and Difficult}
\label{ch:ml-ease}
\hlchaptermodality{96}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can say that something is easy or difficult.}

From cold: the pair, and the welding of a word ending in anusvara onto aaNu, which the learner has been performing since near the beginning without being shown it.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[eḷuppaṁ]{\ml{എളുപ്പം} (eḷuppaṁ) — easy}

\label{lesson:ML-C96-eluppam}



\begin{quote}
Say \emph{this}. Then say the little word that finishes a sentence by saying something \textbf{is} so.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{What to know first}
\textbf{\ml{എളുപ്പം}} — \emph{eḷuppaṁ} — \textbf{easy.}

\begin{quote}
\textbf{\ml{ഇത്} \ml{എളുപ്പമാണ്}.} — \emph{itŭ eḷuppamāṇŭ} — \textquotedblleft{}\textbf{This is easy.}\textquotedblright{}
\end{quote}

\begin{cousinweb}
The word ends in \textbf{\ml{ം}}, and you have been told before that a word ending that way \textbf{says in advance how it will behave}. Here is another thing it says.

Put \textbf{\ml{ആണ്}} after it and the two run together:

\textbf{\ml{എളുപ്പം} + \ml{ആണ്} $\to$ \ml{എളുപ്പമാണ്}}

\textbf{Nothing happens to the sound.} That \textbf{\ml{ം}} is already the sound \textbf{m}, and it stays exactly that. What changes is the \emph{writing}: once \textbf{\ml{ആണ്}} puts a vowel behind it, the \textbf{m} needs the full letter \textbf{\ml{മ}} to carry that vowel, and \textbf{\ml{ം}} cannot.

Say the two words one after the other, quickly. \textbf{You will not hear anything change} — which is why you have been doing this for most of the book without noticing:

\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{} & \textbf{} \\
\midrule
\textbf{\ml{സുഖമാണ്}} & \emph{(I am) well} \\
\textbf{\ml{ഇഷ്ടമാണ്}} & \emph{(I) like it} \\
\textbf{\ml{മോശമാണ്}} & \emph{(it) is bad} \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

Every one of those is a word ending in \textbf{\ml{ം}} with \textbf{\ml{ആണ്}} welded on.

\textbf{You were shown this once, at \ml{മോശം}.} Here it is again — and this time it is not a fact about one word you were given. \textbf{It is something you do}, to a word you met a minute ago.
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{eḷuppaṁ}
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{eḷuppamāṇŭ}
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{itŭ eḷuppamāṇŭ}
  \item \emph{Look:} at \textbf{\ml{സുഖമാണ്}} and \textbf{\ml{എളുപ്പമാണ്}}, and find the part that is the same
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What is \emph{easy}? (\textbf{\ml{എളുപ്പം}}.) What happens to its \textbf{\ml{ം}} when \textbf{\ml{ആണ്}} arrives? (\textbf{It gets written as \ml{മ}} — because a vowel now follows it. The sound does not change.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[prayāsaṁ]{\ml{പ്രയാസം} (prayāsaṁ) — difficult}

\label{lesson:ML-C96-prayaasam}



\begin{quote}
Say \emph{this is easy}. All of it, in one breath.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{What to know first}
\textbf{\ml{പ്രയാസം}} — \emph{prayāsaṁ} — \textbf{difficult.}

\begin{quote}
\textbf{\ml{ഇത്} \ml{പ്രയാസമാണ്}.} — \emph{itŭ prayāsamāṇŭ} — \textquotedblleft{}\textbf{This is difficult.}\textquotedblright{}
\end{quote}

\textbf{It ends in \ml{ം} as well}, so it behaves the way the last one did, and you did not have to be told a second time.

\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{} & \textbf{} \\
\midrule
\textbf{\ml{ഇത്} \ml{എളുപ്പമാണ്}} & this is easy \\
\textbf{\ml{ഇത്} \ml{പ്രയാസമാണ്}} & this is difficult \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

\textbf{One word apart, and the sentence is the opposite.} Everything around it holds still.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
This is a pair you can say about anything you can point at — a word, a letter, a road, a lesson. It is also the first thing most learners want to say about the language itself, and \textbf{you can now say it in the language}, which is a better place to complain from.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{prayāsaṁ}
  \item \emph{itŭ prayāsamāṇŭ}
  \item the two sentences one after the other, and hear where they part
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Easy and difficult? (\textbf{\ml{എളുപ്പം}, \ml{പ്രയാസം}}.) Did the second one need a new rule? (\textbf{No} — it ends the same way, so it behaves the same way.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[eḷuppavuṁ prayāsavuṁ enna ōrmma]{(easy, difficult) — from cold}

\label{lesson:ML-R96-ease-recall}



\begin{quote}
Close the lessons before this one. Say \emph{this is easy}, then say the opposite.
\end{quote}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: the welding was already yours}]
\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{} & \textbf{} \\
\midrule
\textbf{\ml{ഇത്} \ml{എളുപ്പമാണ്}} & this is easy \\
\textbf{\ml{ഇത്} \ml{പ്രയാസമാണ്}} & this is difficult \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

Two new words, and \textbf{no new grammar at all.} Both end in \textbf{\ml{ം}}, and a word ending in \textbf{\ml{ം}} welds onto \textbf{\ml{ആണ്}}: the \textbf{m} sound stays exactly where it was, and only its spelling changes, because a vowel now follows it.

You were doing it long before this chapter:

\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{} & \textbf{} \\
\midrule
\textbf{\ml{സുഖമാണ്}} & well \\
\textbf{\ml{ഇഷ്ടമാണ്}} & liked \\
\textbf{\ml{മോശമാണ്}} & bad \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

\textbf{It was named once, at \ml{മോശം}}, and it never had to become a rule you carried, because you had no word of your own to put through it. \textbf{Now you have two}, and the pattern stops being a fact about somebody else's word.
\end{grammarlens}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
A judgement you can make about anything you can point at.

It is worth noticing what the chapter did \textbf{not} need. No new arrangement, no new ending, no exception. \textbf{Two words, dropped into a frame that was already running.} That is what most of this stage looks like now: the language was built first and the vocabulary arrives into it.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{eḷuppaṁ} $\to$ \emph{eḷuppamāṇŭ}
  \item \emph{prayāsaṁ} $\to$ \emph{prayāsamāṇŭ}
  \item \emph{itŭ eḷuppamāṇŭ}
  \item \emph{itŭ prayāsamāṇŭ}
  \item one older word that welds the same way
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Easy and difficult? (\textbf{\ml{എളുപ്പം}, \ml{പ്രയാസം}}.) How is the \textbf{\ml{ം}} written when \textbf{\ml{ആണ്}} follows? (\textbf{As \ml{മ}} — the sound stays the same.) Was that new in this chapter? (\textbf{No} — you had been saying it for most of the book.)
\end{tcolorbox}
